blocks.text: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann of Germany made a startling discovery: when slow-moving neutrons bombard uranium-235, the reaction produces barium-141 and krypton-92 and, on average, three neutrons. The masses of barium and krypton are both less than that of uranium. This reaction differed from other nuclear reactions in two ways: the uranium nucleus breaks into two nuclei of almost equal size, whereas in other reactions the masses of reactants and products differ little; and a very large amount of energy is released.

blocks.title: Fission reaction
blocks.text: A fission reaction is one in which a heavy nucleus, such as uranium, splits into two nuclei of roughly equal size, with the release of energy.

The fission of uranium-235 can be written 235-92-U + 1-0-n -> 141-56-Ba + 92-36-Kr + 3 1-0-n + Q (19.3), where Q is the energy given out. Comparing the total energy on both sides, about 200 MeV is released in the fission of one uranium nucleus. The sums of the mass numbers and of the charge numbers are the same on both sides (Fig 19.2).

The graph of Fig 19.1 explains this. The binding energy per nucleon is about 7.6 MeV for uranium and about 8.5 MeV for the fission products barium and krypton. So when a uranium nucleus breaks into barium and krypton, energy is released at about 8.5 - 7.6 = 0.9 MeV per nucleon: 235 x 0.9 = 211.5 MeV per uranium nucleus. The fission of uranium does not always give the same fragments; many pairs from the flat upper part of the curve can form, for example 235-92-U + 1-0-n -> 132-50-Sn + 101-42-Mo + 3 1-0-n + Q (19.4), or 140-54-Xe + 94-38-Sr + 2 1-0-n + Q (19.5). All the fission fragments are radioactive. Fission also occurs in other heavy elements, but it happens very easily with slow neutrons in uranium-235 and plutonium-239, which are mostly used for fission.

blocks.alt: A slow neutron approaches a uranium-235 nucleus, drawn as a cluster of protons and neutrons; the nucleus absorbs it and becomes an unstable compound nucleus uranium-236, which splits into barium-141 and krypton-92; three neutrons fly out and about 200 MeV is released. Below: 235-92-U + 1-0-n -> 141-56-Ba + 92-36-Kr + 3 1-0-n + Q.
blocks.caption: Fission of uranium-235 (original diagram after Fig 19.2).
blocks.long_description: The two fragments are more tightly bound than the uranium nucleus, so their total mass is slightly less; that lost mass appears as about 200 MeV of energy, mostly as the kinetic energy of the fragments.

blocks.text: In fission, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and breaks into two nuclei of almost equal mass, emitting two or three neutrons. If these neutrons are used properly, they cause fission in more uranium nuclei, so that the reaction maintains itself. This is a fission chain reaction (Fig 19.3). Suppose one slow neutron causes fission in one uranium atom, releasing about three neutrons; if conditions are right, these cause fission in more atoms, and in an extremely short time a huge amount of energy, with a huge explosion, is produced.

Conditions can be arranged so that only one neutron from each fission causes another fission, while the others escape or are absorbed by other materials; the chain reaction then proceeds steadily. In a thin sheet of fissile material such as enriched uranium-235 (Fig 19.4 a), the neutrons escape into the air and no chain reaction occurs. Some shapes give more favourable conditions (Fig 19.4 b): a few neutrons cause one more fission, but still no chain reaction. In a sufficiently large sphere of highly fissile material (Fig 19.4 c), most neutrons are absorbed before they escape, and a chain reaction occurs.

blocks.title: Critical mass
blocks.text: Critical mass is the mass of uranium in which one neutron, out of all the neutrons produced in one fission, produces a further fission. Its volume is the critical volume or size.

If the mass of uranium is much greater than the critical mass, the chain reaction proceeds rapidly and a huge explosion results; an atom bomb works on this principle. If the mass is less than the critical mass, the chain reaction does not proceed. If it equals the critical mass, the chain reaction proceeds at a steady rate, giving a steady source of energy; this is the principle of a nuclear reactor. In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled by rods, usually of cadmium, inserted into the reactor. Cadmium absorbs many neutrons without becoming unstable or radioactive, so inserting the rods cuts down the number of neutrons available for fission.

blocks.alt: Top: a branching tree; one nucleus at the left sends two neutrons to two nuclei, each of which sends two more, and so on, the number of fissions doubling at each step. Bottom: three panels; a thin sheet from which neutrons escape; an arch-shaped piece in which one neutron causes one more fission but others escape; a large orange sphere (critical) in which neutrons from several fissions are absorbed inside and cause further fissions.
blocks.caption: Fission chain reaction and critical mass (original diagram after Figs 19.3 and 19.4).
blocks.long_description: Whether the chain grows, stays steady or dies out depends on how many neutrons from each fission go on to cause another. A small or thin piece loses too many neutrons through its surface.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: In a controlled chain reaction only one neutron, on average, from each fission event causes another nucleus to fission. As a result, energy is released at a steady, controlled rate.
